He pointed out that nine deaths had been recorded just a day earlier.
The overall situation, he said, needed to be assessed through sustained trends in infections, hospital admissions and fatalities rather than a single day’s figures.
Bari stressed the importance of expanding vaccination coverage, saying approximately 60 million children under the age of 15 needed to be immunised to bring the outbreak fully under control.
He also called for stronger protection against childhood pneumonia and diarrhoeal diseases, alongside measles vaccination.
Children who had missed routine immunisation should be identified and vaccinated promptly, while those already infected must receive appropriate medical treatment without delay, he said.
Health experts emphasised that continued vaccination, early diagnosis, effective hospital care and public awareness would be essential to sustaining the improvement and preventing further deaths.

item.title: Salt is turning Bangladesh’s coast into a place people leave
item.description:
In the villages of Satkhira and Khulna, you taste salt on the wind. Older residents remember when the breeze carried the scent of ripening paddy.
Today, many of those fields hold saline water used for shrimp farming. What may appear to be an economic opportunity has also contributed to the gradual loss of farmland and traditional livelihoods for many families.
Salinity is no longer a seasonal nuisance in the coastal south; it is a chronic condition. It is not confined to Khulna and Satkhira.
In neighboring Barisal division alone, 415,000 hectares, or 52% of cultivable land, were affected by salinity in 2024. When the sea spills into a village, it stays. It ruins crops, freshwater ponds, and shallow aquifers, and the damage lasts for years.
The cause is not only climate change.
Sea levels are rising, and tidal surges keep eroding the coast, but local farmers also say that shrimp enclosures pump saline water into neighboring rice fields. The expansion of shrimp farming, particularly where saline water is allowed to spread beyond designated enclosures, has added to the problem.
Climate pressure and local land-use choices have worked together, and any serious response must address both.
In Dacope, sodium in drinking water is significantly associated with pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension among women.
An estimated 73% of residents in five coastal upazilas of Khulna and Satkhira drink unsafe saline water. For women who walk long distances just to find safe drinking water, salinity is a daily, compounding risk.
Cyclones such as Sidr, Aila and Amphan have devastated coastal livelihoods.
Although emergency relief provides temporary assistance, many communities continue to struggle with damaged homes, farmland and infrastructure long after the storms have passed. Embankments broken by the surge are not always rebuilt to last, and when saltwater enters farmland, it can take years to recover.
For a smallholder or a fisher, that recovery is often out of reach. Savings run out, and families leave.
Unlike sudden disasters such as cyclones, rising soil salinity gradually makes it harder for people to sustain their livelihoods.
Research suggests that this slow deterioration is also linked to increased internal migration , with nearly 200,000 coastal residents potentially forced to move. Most would stay within their own district, while the poorest often cannot afford to leave at all.
Some end up in the slums of Dhaka or Chittagong. A man who owned a small plot and a pond in Dacope or Shyamnagar may end up pulling a rickshaw or carrying bricks. His wife may work as a domestic helper, and their children grow up far from the village.
The loss is not only economic; families and entire communities are scattered.
National figures do not isolate salinity as a cause, but they show the pressure on a coast where slow salt damage is repeatedly finished off by storms and floods. Between 2008 and 2025, disasters caused more than 21 million internal displacements in Bangladesh.
These are movements, not unique individuals, and many were pre-emptive cyclone evacuations. Even so, the trend is clear: displacements peaked in 2019, driven by major floods, and again in 2020, driven by floods and Cyclone Amphan.
Projections for the decades ahead are worse. According to the World Bank, internal climate migration in Bangladesh could reach 13.3 million by 2050 under one pessimistic scenario.
A subsequent 2021 update estimated that the figure could rise to 19.9 million. The drivers are falling crop yields, water scarcity, and sea-level rise. Metropolitan centres like Dhaka are already stretched and cannot absorb millions more.
Bangladesh contributes less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it bears some of the heaviest consequences.
Climate finance has not matched the need.
The National Adaptation Plan puts the cost at about $230 billion by 2050, or roughly $8.5 billion a year. Between 2009 and 2022, however, the country received only about $268 million in grants from the Green Climate Fund, the Adaptation Fund and the LDC Fund combined, not counting loans and domestic spending. Meanwhile, the new Fund for responding to Loss and Damage has set aside just $250 million for its initial phase, for all eligible countries. These figures highlight the gap between the resources available and the scale of adaptation and recovery Bangladesh needs.
Protecting the Sundarbans must be a priority. The forest is estimated to have cut Cyclone Amphan’s wind speed by roughly 70 kilometres an hour and lowered the surge by three to four feet.
But rising salinity, reduced upstream freshwater flow and illegal logging are degrading this natural shield. At the same time, investment must flow into village-level adaptation: salt-tolerant rice varieties, rainwater harvesting systems and dry-season drinking water infrastructure.
The crisis also demands firmer control over land use. Where enclosures deliberately flood surrounding farmland with saline water, local governments must have the authority to regulate shrimp farming.
Shrimp production in five major coastal districts fell by more than 7% between 2018-19 and 2022-23, and some farmers are returning to rice and other crops. This shift deserves policy support, but it must also recognize that shrimp farming remains an important source of income for many coastal households.
Any transition needs credit, technical support, and a fair transition for those who work the enclosures.
Finally, economic resilience within the coastal belt, through cottage industries, climate-resilient aquaculture and poultry farming, needs real financing, so that residents can choose to stay rather than be forced to migrate.
None of this will happen without sustained pressure.
Young people, local environmental organizations and journalists have a critical role in keeping the coast at the top of the policy agenda and holding international partners to their funding promises.
But responsibility cannot rest on local communities alone. Government agencies, businesses, and international partners must work together to protect coastal livelihoods and make adaptation a long-term priority. The coast will not save itself, but action at every level of government and society still can.
AL Sharia is an environmental activist and a student of Disaster Science and Management at Begum Rokeya University, Rangpur.

item.title: Nilkhet’s piracy problem: The cost of affordable education
item.description:
For generations, Nilkhet book market has been synonymous with affordable textbooks for university students. From law and medicine to engineering and business studies, students can often find books at prices far below those of original imported editions.
But behind this affordability is a long-running copyright problem: the reproduction and commercial sale of books without the permission of authors or copyright owners.
Nilkhet has long been known as a major centre for pirated books. A textbook that costs Tk200 in its original form, for instance, may be sold for around Tk80 as a pirated copy.
Two decades later, the problem has not disappeared. A 2024 investigation reported that industry insiders estimated that at least 400,000 pirated books were sold annually, with books reproduced through downloading, scanning, and photocopying.
The issue raises a difficult question: how can Bangladesh protect authors and publishers without making essential educational materials unaffordable for students?
Bangladesh's copyright laws protect literary works, including books, and recognise authors' rights over how their work is reproduced and distributed. Commercially reproducing an entire textbook without permission and selling the copies can amount to copyright infringement. Those involved in such activities may face fines, imprisonment, and the confiscation of illegally reproduced books.
However, copyright protection does not mean that every form of copying is illegal. The law recognises certain exceptions for educational purposes, research, criticism and review.
These provisions acknowledge that access to knowledge and the protection of intellectual property must coexist.
The distinction lies in how copyrighted material is used. Using a reasonable portion of a book for educational purposes is different from reproducing an entire commercial textbook in large quantities and selling it for profit. An educational purpose alone does not justify unlimited copying.
This distinction is particularly important in Nilkhet, where the issue is not simply whether students photocopy materials, but whether businesses commercially reproduce and distribute copyrighted books without authorisation.
Authorities have acted against piracy in the market, yet enforcement has not eliminated the problem. The continued availability of copied textbooks suggests that the market is driven by strong demand as well as commercial incentives.
Copyright is not simply about books as physical objects; it protects the intellectual labour and authorship behind those works. When unauthorised copies replace legitimate sales, authors and publishers can lose royalties and revenue.
At the same time, treating every student who purchases a cheap copy as equivalent to a commercial pirate would ignore Bangladesh's economic reality.
Many students turn to Nilkhet because original foreign textbooks can cost several times more than their affordable alternatives. For students on limited budgets, these cheaper copies are often a practical way to access the materials required for their studies.
Addressing the problem therefore requires a distinction between students seeking affordable learning resources and businesses profiting from unauthorised reproduction. Enforcement should focus on organised reproduction and large-scale commercial distribution, while the government, universities and publishers should expand lawful access to educational materials.
Publishers could offer low-cost student editions, affordable digital books, institutional licences and authorised photocopying schemes. Universities could negotiate bulk licences and strengthen libraries so students can access expensive textbooks without relying on pirated copies.
Nilkhet's experience shows that copyright enforcement and access to education do not have to be opposing goals.
Bangladesh needs a system that protects authors from commercial piracy while ensuring that the price of lawful educational materials does not place essential knowledge beyond the reach of ordinary students. The real challenge is not choosing between copyright and education. It is finding a legal and affordable way to protect both.
Sumaiya Rifat Anika studies law at Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP).

item.title: Two youths shot, stabbed in Hatirjheel
item.description:
Two youths were injured in a shooting and stabbing attack allegedly carried out by a group of criminals in the Bagichar Tek area of Wapda Road under Hatirjheel Police Station in the capital on Monday afternoon.
The attack took place in front of Kader's rickshaw garage around noon.
The injured were identified as Salauddin Babu and Sharif, 28. Both are autorickshaw drivers.
They were initially taken to Mugda General Hospital before being transferred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) in the evening.
Salauddin sustained multiple stab wounds to different parts of his body, as well as gunshot injuries to his leg and chest. Sharif suffered a stab wound to his right leg.
Salauddin said seven to eight people, including Hasnain, Hasib and Nuru, members of the local Tokai Sujan group, intercepted him and attacked him with sharp weapons and firearms. They also snatched Tk26,000 from him.
He added that the same group attacked Sharif, leaving him injured.
Salauddin said he had lived in the area since childhood and knew many local residents. However, he could not say why he was targeted.
He had previously lived in Qatar and returned to Bangladesh two months ago. He is the son of Barok Sheikh of Paisa Bankai village in Gournadi upazila of Barisal. He had been staying at the rickshaw garage on Wapda Road.
Sharif is the son of Belal Hossain of Kutum Pukur village in Chandina upazila of Comilla. He also lives in the area.
Sub-Inspector Md Selim of the DMCH police outpost confirmed the incident, saying the injured were receiving treatment in the hospital's emergency department.

item.title: Brick Kiln Tracker launched to show which kilns harm public health most
item.description:
Where are the brick kilns most harmful to public health located? A new digital platform now lets the public find out. The Brick Kiln Tracker, available at www.iterbhata.com , shows each kiln's location, type (zigzag or fixed chimney) and level of health harm.
Research organization ARCED Foundation and the National University of Singapore (NUS) jointly launched the tracker on Monday. It was unveiled at The Westin Dhaka at an event titled "Public Action for Cleaner Air: Launching the Brick Kiln Tracker." Speakers shared this information at the event.
The speakers said brick kilns are one of the main sources of air pollution in Bangladesh. In controlling this pollution, the country's general public, media workers and civil society also have an important role to play alongside the Department of Environment (DoE).
Through the tracker, journalists, researchers, civil society and local residents will be able to find out which kilns pose the greatest risk to health.
The public tracker was launched to put information on the health harm of brick kilns within everyone's reach. According to Dr Martin Mattsson, assistant professor at NUS and head of the research initiative, knowing where kilns are located and how much harm each causes makes it easier to prioritize the most harmful ones and take appropriate steps.
A small number of brick kilns are responsible for a large share of the total health harm. So even reducing pollution emitted from just these kilns would protect many people from health risks, researchers believe.
As soon as winter sets in, air pollution in Dhaka rises sharply. Dhaka ranks among the world's most polluted cities almost every year.
According to the Air Quality Life Index (AQLI) 2025 report, Bangladesh has the most polluted air in the world. Air pollution levels are 12 times higher than the WHO recommended level and almost twice as high as the government's own national air standard.
While tobacco use cuts the average life expectancy of people in Bangladesh by about 2 years, air pollution is estimated to cut it by about 5.5 years. In Dhaka district, this loss stands at about 7 years of life expectancy.
Coal-fired brick kilns are among the main sources of this pollution. The country has more than 6,000 brick kilns, which operate mainly from November to May. During winter, polluted air from these kilns gets trapped over nearby densely populated areas, posing a threat to the health of the people living there.
According to scientists, air pollution causes various lung diseases and deadly illnesses, including lung cancer, stroke and heart attack.
The extent of a kiln's harm depends on its technology and location. Bangladesh generally has two types of kiln technology: fixed chimney and zigzag. Both are harmful, but fixed chimney kilns are comparatively more harmful.
Kilns located close to densely populated areas are comparatively more harmful to public health, as their pollution reaches a larger number of people. When smoke from the same type of kiln drifts toward less populated areas, the harm is comparatively lower.
That is why, in calculating each kiln's health harm, the tracker takes into account the kiln's technology, the wind direction, atmospheric chemistry, and the population density of the surrounding areas the polluted air reaches.
For example, the brick kilns of Savar upazila are located northwest of Dhaka city. In winter, polluted air emitted from these kilns flows over densely populated Dhaka city. As a result, these kilns are extremely harmful to public health and are marked as "most harmful" on the tracker.
In the tracker, each brick kiln's precise location (latitude and longitude), type (zigzag or fixed chimney) and level of health harm are listed, ranked from lowest to highest harm. It works mainly in two steps.
Identification: Using satellite imagery and a machine-learning model, every brick kiln in the country is located, its type identified, and it is recorded whether it was active during the past year's brick season.
Measuring harm: Using the "ORBIT" air quality model, the kiln's type, weather, wind direction and the population density of surrounding areas are analyzed to calculate the estimated annual health harm caused by each kiln.
The Brick Kiln Tracker is being rolled out in phases. The current pilot phase covers 168 upazilas across 44 districts.
Researchers from the National University of Singapore, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Nottingham and ARCED Foundation jointly developed the Brick Kiln Tracker. The head of the research team is Dr Martin Mattsson, assistant professor at the National University of Singapore.
The initiative received support from the National University of Singapore, the University of Nottingham, Development Innovation Ventures, Open Road Impact, Coefficient Giving, the Mercatus Center and the International Growth Centre (IGC).

item.title: Bus set on fire in Mirpur
item.description:
A passenger bus operated by Basumati Paribahan was set on fire by miscreants in front of Sony Cinema Hall in Mirpur 1, Dhaka, at around 7:45pm on Monday.
The Fire Service headquarters confirmed the incident.
Police said miscreants had set fire to a Basumati Paribahan bus. Those involved in the incident would be brought to justice, police added.

item.title: EU takes no position on calls to label Awami League ‘terrorist group’
item.description:
The European Union has no official position on calls to designate the Awami League a terrorist organisation, EU Ambassador to Bangladesh Michael Miller said on Monday, stressing that accountability for past human rights violations must be pursued through the rule of law.
Speaking at a DCAB Talk organised by the Diplomatic Correspondents Association, Bangladesh (DCAB) at the National Press Club in Dhaka, Miller said the EU wanted Bangladesh to remain stable, with justice, public safety and the rejection of violence at the centre of that process.
Responding to a question about demands from some quarters to declare the Awami League a terrorist organisation, the ambassador said the EU had not adopted an official position on the issue.
He said the EU had observed measures taken by the interim government and subsequent developments, but emphasised that accountability for past abuses must be consistent with respect for the rule of law.
Miller also stressed the importance of renouncing violence and maintaining public order and safety.
The ambassador said the EU closely monitored Bangladesh’s human rights situation, which remained an important factor in determining the scope and ambition of bilateral relations.
He acknowledged that Bangladesh had made progress in some areas but said considerable room for improvement remained.
Whenever human rights protections came under pressure, the EU raised the issue through discussions involving the European Parliament, member states and its headquarters, he said.
The ambassador added that the EU continued to engage with civil society organisations, institutions, parliamentarians and government ministers to promote improvements.
He also referred to the reform commissions established under the interim government, saying they had produced several constructive proposals.
Miller said the EU intended to continue engaging with the government to support the implementation of those initiatives.
Responding to a question about press freedom, Miller stressed the need for responsible journalism during Bangladesh’s political transition.
He described the period as critical and said the media had an important role in ensuring that developments were reported responsibly.
The ambassador also observed that the government had maintained control over the security situation.
Turning to economic relations, Miller warned that Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry could face growing competitive pressure as labour costs rise and preferential access to European markets changes.
He said the sector’s current competitiveness depended significantly on relatively low labour costs, an advantage that could weaken as Bangladesh’s demographic and economic conditions evolved.
The ambassador noted that several of Bangladesh’s competitors had already secured free trade agreements with the EU, putting them in a stronger position in the European market.
Following Bangladesh’s graduation from least developed country status and the expiry of the relevant transition period, its garment exports could face most-favoured-nation tariffs unless alternative preferential arrangements were secured.
Such a shift, he warned, could substantially affect the sector’s competitiveness.
Miller called for early planning, technological modernisation and greater investment in sustainable production, including circular economy practices and renewable energy.
He said these changes would require years of investment, infrastructure development and implementation, making it essential for Bangladesh to begin discussions with the EU on future trade arrangements without delay.
The ambassador reaffirmed the EU’s willingness to work with Bangladesh’s government, private sector and civil society to ensure a smooth and predictable economic transition.
He said relations between Bangladesh and the EU were evolving beyond the traditional donor-recipient framework towards a broader partnership based on shared interests.
Despite existing challenges, Miller expressed optimism about the future of bilateral relations.
He added that his decision to extend his tenure in Bangladesh reflected his commitment to strengthening that partnership.

item.title: RMG wage deadlock persists as owners, workers fail to agree
item.description:
The readymade garment (RMG) sector's minimum wage deadlock continued on Monday as factory owners and workers failed to reach an agreement at the third meeting of the Minimum Wage Board, with no revised pay structure announced.
Both sides have been asked to submit fresh proposals after workers' representatives rejected the employers' initial offer as inadequate, while owners considered the workers' demand excessive.
Board Chairman Syed Azad Subhani disclosed the decision at a press briefing at the board's office in Segunbagicha after the meeting.
He said the board would consider the revised proposals before making a recommendation. Board members, however, declined to disclose the amount offered by employers.
Workers' representative Babul Akhter said the employers' initial offer was too low and unacceptable, just as the owners viewed the workers' earlier proposal as excessive. He said both sides were willing to revise their positions to find a compromise.
At the board's second meeting, Babul proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk32,000. Meanwhile, garment workers' organisations have been demanding at least Tk30,000 a month.
The current minimum monthly wage for garment workers is Tk12,500, announced in November 2023 and effective from December that year. The previous minimum wage, set in 2018, was Tk8,000.
The renewed wage negotiations come amid weeks of labour unrest across major garment-producing areas, including Mirpur, Gazipur, Savar and Ashulia. Workers have staged demonstrations, blocked roads and stopped work, while clashes and factory shutdowns have disrupted production.
Workers have cited rising living costs, including food prices, house rent and healthcare expenses, as reasons for seeking a substantial increase. The unrest has also highlighted broader concerns over workers' living standards and the gap between wages and the cost of living.
Babul urged workers to return to work and keep production running while negotiations continue.
Subhani said the board was weighing employers' ability to pay, the condition of small and medium-sized enterprises, inflation, market prices, export competitiveness and workers' demands. He expressed hope that a recommendation could be finalised within one or two more meetings.
The board's statutory tenure runs until April 30. After its recommendation is finalised and gazetted, the law provides 14 days for opinions or objections.
Meanwhile, workers from several labour organisations, including the Sammilito Garment Sramik Federation, staged a protest and formed a human chain outside the board's office on Monday, reiterating their demand for a Tk30,000 minimum wage.
The six-member Minimum Wage Board was formed on November 1. It is chaired by District and Sessions Judge Syed Azad Subhani, with Dhaka University Public Administration Professor Dr Mosleh Uddin Ahmed serving as the neutral member.
The employers' representatives are Bangladesh Employers' Federation Joint Secretary General Asif Ayub and BGMEA Director ABM Shamsuddin. The workers' representatives are Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal President Anwar Hossain and Bangladesh Garments and Industrial Workers Federation General Secretary Babul Akhter.

item.title: PM urges parties to stay united to protect sovereignty and democracy
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has called on political parties to remain united in protecting the country's interests, independence, sovereignty and democracy amid the current political situation, stressing the importance of maintaining the anti-fascist alliance.
He made the remarks during a meeting with senior leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) at the Secretariat on Monday, following recent incidents of cocktail explosions, arson and violence in different parts of the country.
The meeting discussed the current political situation, national unity, state reforms, justice and sovereignty. Following the meeting, the prime minister hosted a lunch for the NCP delegation.
Prime Minister's Office spokesperson Mahdi Amin told reporters that the anti-fascist national unity would remain intact despite differences in political views, ideologies and principles.
He said all pro-democracy political forces remained united in protecting the country's independence, sovereignty, democracy and people's rights.
"Under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, the government wants to move forward with the democratic journey and build a self-reliant Bangladesh, with all political forces working shoulder to shoulder," Mahdi said.
He said the issue of unity in the interest of the people and the country was given significant importance during the meeting.
Mahdi urged everyone to remain vigilant so that the forces of the ousted authoritarian regime, operating from abroad, could not create instability in Bangladesh.
He said democratic political parties and anti-fascist forces remained united against the violence and sabotage carried out by the fallen regime, adding that the meeting aimed to convey this message of unity to the public.
Recalling the July 2024 mass uprising, Mahdi said people from all walks of life, irrespective of class, profession, religion, ethnicity, political views and ideology, had come together with the aspiration to build a Bangladesh where human rights, the rule of law and freedom of expression would be ensured, and democratic aspirations against fascism would be fulfilled.
He said the meeting reflected those aspirations.
"The Liberation War of 1971 was a struggle to achieve independence, while the 2024 mass uprising was a movement to establish independence, human rights and people's rights," he said.
He stressed the need to prioritise national interests, sovereignty and the rights of the people under the principle of "Bangladesh First" to move the country forward.
Mahdi said socioeconomic development, protection of industries and employment generation were important issues concerning national interests and required political consensus.
Asked whether the meeting had discussed a fresh initiative to establish political unity, Mahdi Amin said national unity had already been established through the July-August mass uprising.
He said unity among pro-democracy political forces had been built on the principle that the people are the owners of the state, adding that the government wanted to further strengthen that unity.
Regarding reforms, Mahdi said the government's position was clear. The prime minister had stated in parliament that the commitments made in the BNP's election manifesto and through signing the July Charter would be implemented in full, including the provisions accompanied by notes of dissent.
"There will be no deviation from these commitments," he said.
He said nearly 100 ordinances had been converted into laws during the first session of Parliament following the formation of the government, describing reform as an ongoing process.
He said the government was advancing reforms in line with its electoral pledges.
The NCP proposed giving national unity a long-term framework. Party Convener Nahid Islam said unity should not be limited to immediate political crises or the situation surrounding December.
He said a roadmap was needed to address issues involving the Awami League and Bangladesh-India relations in the long term.
Nahid said the NCP had urged the government to bring together political and social forces involved in the July uprising and develop a common approach to addressing the country's long-term challenges.
The government assured the party that its proposals would be considered, he said, adding that the success of the talks would depend on concrete actions.
Nahid said the NCP did not want discussions for the sake of discussions, stressing that the outcome would depend on the steps taken by the government and whether it could earn public confidence.
He said the meeting discussed ways to overcome the current situation, establish political unity and maintain the anti-fascist stance.
The prime minister called on political parties to remain united around the spirit of the July mass uprising and their opposition to fascism, he added.
However, Nahid alleged that the current situation had emerged due to the government's failure over the past seven to eight months to control law and order, ensure justice, take a firm stance against the Awami League and clarify its diplomatic approach towards India.
He said reforms, justice and sovereignty must be prioritised in any national unity initiative, recommending that reform be included as a key agenda in the process.
The NCP called for members of the Constitution Reform Council to take their oath to initiate the reform process.
Nahid also called for strengthening the capacity of the International Crimes Tribunal, expediting investigations and submitting charge sheets in cases filed over the July uprising, and taking steps to bring former prime minister Sheikh Hasina back from India to implement the court's verdict.
The party also demanded security and rehabilitation for participants in the July uprising and the return of those involved in the murder of Osman Hadi.
On Bangladesh-India relations, Nahid alleged that India was allowing the Awami League to use its territory to destabilise Bangladesh.
He called for a united political resistance against Indian hegemony and urged the government to take a firm position in negotiations over the renewal of the Ganges water-sharing treaty, which is set to expire on December 12, to ensure Bangladesh's fair share of water.
Proposing a long-term framework for national unity and a common foreign policy to protect the country's sovereignty and security, Nahid said Bangladesh needed a unified national foreign policy on issues of regional dominance instead of party-based foreign policies.
He said the NCP would continue its struggle for democracy, sovereignty and economic security from its own position and wanted to move forward with the government and the people.
The meeting began at 1:20pm in the Cabinet Division's conference room at the Secretariat and lasted around 40 minutes.
The NCP delegation was led by Convener Nahid Islam and included Member Secretary Akhtar Hossain, Senior Joint Convener Hasnat Abdullah and Joint Convener Akram Hossain.
Prime Minister's Education and Labour Adviser Mahdi Amin and Chief Whip of Parliament Mia Nuruddin Ahmed Apu were also present.

item.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after US government input
item.description:
Nvidia on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after input from senior US government officials left its board confident he posed no national security risk, less than two weeks after the co-founder resigned due to an alleged spy scandal.
President Donald Trump welcomed the move as a “correct and proper decision.”
The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately, after a series of meetings left directors satisfied with his “candor and ability to lead,” the company said in a statement.
Nvidia did not name the government officials it consulted or say what they told the board.
The decision came three days after Trump publicly urged Nvidia to take Huang back, calling him “one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world” and saying he would “love to see Jensen be given a second chance.”
Trump described Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions,” and said the company should rehire him “if they were smart.”
Huang had offered to return, but the board initially refused.
Board chair Harvey Jones had said on an earnings call last week that directors had unanimously accepted his resignation and did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said, thanking the board, staff, shareholders and his family. “I can’t wait to get back to work.”
Huang, 63, stepped down on November 12 following reports that he had a relationship with Alice Huang -- no relation -- a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips.
US intelligence services reportedly concluded she passed information to Beijing, which has denied the allegations.
Board chair Harvey Jones said Monday that directors now believe Huang “is the right person to lead Nvidia” and that his return serves the interests of shareholders, employees, partners and customers.
Jones, a former Synopsys chief executive who was named Nvidia’s first-ever board chair during the crisis, will stay in the role. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as CFO.
Nvidia said a committee of independent directors set up earlier this month to investigate whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort will see its probe through to the end. Huang supports the investigation and has committed to cooperating, the company said.

item.title: Employers submit RMG minimum wage proposal
item.description:
Garment factory owners submitted their proposal for the new minimum wage of readymade garment (RMG) workers on Monday, though the Minimum Wage Board declined to disclose the proposed figure while negotiations continue.
Speaking to reporters after the board’s third meeting on November 23, board chairman Syed Azad Subhani said the session began at 11:30am and continued into the evening with representatives from both sides alongside sector experts.
Following the workers' formal proposal at the second meeting, the board is now reviewing arguments and counterarguments from both parties.
Subhani noted that the board unanimously decided not to reveal the owners' proposed amount until discussions conclude, urging the public to ignore unverified figures circulating on social media.
He emphasized that the board is prioritizing the interests of the sector’s roughly 4 million workers while balancing inflation, living costs, owners’ financial capacity, the condition of small and medium factories, and global competitiveness.
Field data collected from factories across Dhaka, Savar, Ashulia, Narayanganj, and Chittagong was also presented at Monday's meeting to ensure a legally sound and fair decision.
However, workers’ representative Babul Akhter dismissed the owners' initial offer as "unreasonable and inadequate," stating it falls nowhere near the workers’ demands.
"The owners started with a low offer, but this is not final," Akhter told journalists after the meeting.
He added that both sides are expected to revise their proposals to reach a satisfactory consensus.
Recalling the 2023 wage review -- where workers demanded Tk23,000, owners initially offered around Tk10,400, and the wage was eventually fixed at Tk12,500 -- Akhter urged reporters not to publish unconfirmed figures while negotiations remain fluid.
Both the board chairman and the workers' representative indicated a push to wrap up the process quickly.
While the board's legal tenure runs until April 30, Subhani said they aim to finalize the wage in fewer meetings than in previous years, noting that a mandatory 14-day window for objections will follow the final recommendation before a gazette is issued.
Akhter added that workers are prepared to negotiate late into the night or reconvene Tuesday morning to settle the issue swiftly.
Meanwhile, despite ongoing labor unrest since early November, Akhter urged workers to return to work and keep production running.
While expressing sympathy for workers struggling with rising living costs, he stressed that labor organizations do not support halting production and assured that the wage issue will be resolved through the board.

item.title: Clashes between two Awami League groups in Gopalganj leave 20 injured, 4 shot
item.description:
Clashes broke out between two groups over standing arrangements at a gathering of the Awami League, Jubo League and Chhatra League in Gopalganj district on Monday, leaving 20 people injured, including 4 with gunshot wounds.
The incident took place at around 6:30pm in the Launch Ghat Bottola Roundabout area. During the clashes, 6 crude bombs exploded and 10 shops at the Flower Market were vandalised.
According to local sources, leaders and activists of the banned Awami League, Jubo League and Chhatra League brought out a protest procession from the Launch Ghat area in the afternoon.
After the procession, while leaders were delivering speeches at the gathering, a scuffle broke out over standing beside them between Morsalin, a Chhatra League leader from Ghosherchar village, and Sajid, a Chhatra League activist from Charmanikkdah village.
Following the incident, Awami League supporters from the two villages became involved in clashes in the evening. During the clashes, 6 crude bombs exploded, followed by chasing and counter-chasing, gunfire and vandalism. Ten flower shops at the Flower Market were vandalised, and 20 people were injured.
Among those seriously injured are Zahidur Rahman, 19, son of Hafiz Molla, and Sahabul Molla, 35, son of Shafayet Molla, both from Charmanikkdah village, and Zahidul Molla, 37, son of Kabir Molla, from Ghosherchar village.
The injured have been admitted to Gopalganj Sadar Hospital and various other hospitals.
The 4 people shot during the clashes are Pranta Molla, 20, son of Hafiz Molla, his brother Rakib Molla, 22, Sahabul Molla, 35, son of Shafayet Molla, all from the same village, and Amin Molla, 20, son of Tulu Molla, from Charmanikkdah village.
They have been admitted to Gopalganj Medical College Hospital.
Besides, Taslim, 28, son of Akubor from Charmanikkdah village, and Samiul Khan, 6, son of Tuhin Khan from the Panchuria area of the town, received primary treatment at Gopalganj General Hospital.
Dr Naim Ferdous of Gopalganj Medical College Hospital said there were signs of pellet gunshot wounds on the bodies of 4 people. They have been sent for X-rays, while the others received primary treatment.
Tamim Molla, owner of Gopalganj Fulghar and Ityadi Fulghar, said the clash started over standing at the front of the procession. Gunfire and crude bomb explosions took place during the clashes. At that time, 10 shops at the Flower Market were vandalised.
Gopalganj Sadar police station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Aminul Islam said: “We have learned about the matter. We are looking into the details. However, no one has filed a complaint at the police station so far.”

item.title: Teen kills grandmother to repay online gambling debt in Chandpur
item.description:
Police have solved the murder of a 65-year-old woman, whose body was found with her hands and legs bound and throat slit at her apartment in Chandpur town, arresting her 16-year-old grandson within 42 hours of the case being filed.
The teenager allegedly killed his grandmother to repay debts incurred through online gambling before fleeing with her gold jewellery and mobile phone.
Additional Superintendent of Police (Administration and Finance) Nadira Noor disclosed the details at a press briefing at the Chandpur Superintendent of Police's office around 7pm on Monday.
She said the teenager had planned the murder to obtain money to settle his gambling debts. After his arrest, he confessed to the killing in a statement recorded under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, she added.
Police said Lutfunnahar's body was recovered on the evening of November 18 from a rented apartment on the seventh floor of Nazira Complex in the Jorpukur Par area of JM Sengupta Road in Chandpur town. Her hands and legs were bound, and her throat had been slit.
The 65-year-old had been living alone in the apartment since November 1. She had one son and five daughters. Her daughters occasionally visited her, while her only son lives in Japan.
The arrested teenager is the eldest son of Lutfunnahar's third daughter and a Class VIII student at Munshirhat High School
On November 21, the victim's fourth daughter, Nahida Akter, filed a murder case with Chandpur Sadar Model Police Station.
During the investigation, police identified the grandson's alleged involvement through information technology and intelligence sources. They arrested him in a raid in the Jorpukur Par area around 5:30pm on Sunday, within 42 hours of the case being filed.
Following information provided by the teenager, police recovered the knife allegedly used in the murder from a toilet pipe on the building's seventh floor. They also recovered the stolen gold chain, ring and earrings from beneath a steel wardrobe in his room.
During interrogation, the teenager reportedly told police that he had accumulated a substantial debt through online gambling. To arrange the money needed to repay it, he planned to kill his grandmother.
On the day of the murder, he allegedly entered the apartment under a pretext, tied his grandmother's hands and mouth, and slit her throat with a sharp knife before fleeing with her jewellery and mobile phone.
Nadira Noor said the teenager was produced before a court, where he gave a confessional statement under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He was subsequently sent to a juvenile correctional centre.

item.title: Bangladesh skittled as South Africa take control of 2nd Test
item.description:
South Africa's fast bowlers sent Bangladesh crashing to 91 all out as the home team took command on the first day of the second Test at SuperSport Park on Monday.
South Africa were 88 for one in reply at the end of a rain-shortened day, just three runs behind.
Marco Jansen and Kagiso Rabada took three wickets each while Anrich Nortje used express pace to bowl two top-order batsmen in the space of three balls.
"There wasn't much swing and the wicket is on the slow side," insisted Nortje despite Bangladesh's collapse.
"So it was just to try to make them play as much as possible."
It was the lowest first-innings total in Test matches at Centurion.
Bangladesh's miseries were compounded when they were on the wrong end of two decisions early in the South African innings -- and then dropped a catch.
South African captain Aiden Markram was given out leg before wicket against Shoriful Islam in the second over but escaped on review because the ball pitched marginally outside the line of leg stump.
In the next over Taskin Ahmed appealed passionately for a leg-before decision against first Test century-maker Marques Ackerman, who was on one.
Ackerman was given not out and Bangladesh did not seek a review. Replays showed the ball had pitched in line and would have hit the stumps.
Markram and Ackerman put on 49 for the first wicket before Markram was caught behind for 21 off Ebadot Hossain's first ball of the match.
Bangladesh missed another opportunity when new batsman Zubayr Hamza was dropped at first slip by Towhid Hridoy off Khaled Ahmed when he was on two.
Ackerman (46 not out) and Hamza (nine not out) saw South Africa through to the close.
South Africa sent Bangladesh in to bat on a well-grassed pitch after the start of play was delayed by three hours and 40 minutes because of rain.
It took South Africa just 33.3 overs to bowl out the tourists and put themselves into a strong position to push for a 2-0 series sweep.
Jansen had Tanzid Hasan caught at first slip in the second over.
Mahfijul Islam (23) and Mominul Haque (18) put on 34 for the second wicket before Nortje bowled Mahfijul and captain Najmul Hossain Shanto in his second over, beating both batsmen with sheer pace.
Rabada had a spell of three wickets for one run after tea as Bangladesh lost their last five wickets for six runs.
Nortje acknowledged that there was more help for the bowlers than in the first Test when Bangladesh scored 400 in the first innings before losing by nine wickets.
"The conditions were very different," he said.

item.title: AB de Villiers makes new claim about Australian ball-tampering
item.description:
Former South African batsman AB de Villiers has alleged Australia engaged in ball-tampering from the first match of their 2018 "Sandpapergate" tour of South Africa.
De Villiers alleged in a post on his YouTube channel that the ball-tampering, which culminated in Cameron Bancroft being caught using sandpaper in the third Test in Cape Town, actually began in the first Test in Durban.
He also said the Australian bowlers, who have denied any involvement, must have known what was going on.
A fierce debate about the eight-year-old events was triggered in Australia this month when Usman Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the flight of the ball.
Bancroft, who was banned along with captain Steve Smith and David Warner after the incident, said in a recent article that sandpaper was first used in the second Test in Port Elizabeth.
But De Villiers said: "It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE. I'm very happy for people to quote me on that.
"I see everyone is sort of admitting that in Port Elizabeth it also happened. I can very much tell you Durban was no different, in the first Test. Go look at the footage. Absolutely no doubt in my mind."
He added: "We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead. Trust me, I've played a lot of cricket there."
De Villiers added: "So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or (a) nail, I don't care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew. Just stand up and say 'we were wrong'. A lot is at stake now because they lied.
"The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn't just reverse. It's not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, 'guys, we were wrong'."
De Villiers was a central figure in a bad-tempered series. He was run out in Durban and Australian bowler Nathan Lyon appeared to drop the ball on him -- one of several incidents that inflamed tensions during the series.
The then South African captain Faf du Plessis revealed in his autobiography that he had persuaded the normally mild-mannered De Villiers to lead an aggressive response in the second Test to what Du Plessis saw as bullying tactics by Australia.
"I spoke to AB and said that the only way we were going to win the series was if he was willing to lead the fight against the Aussies with me. 'You and I will fight fire with fire. The rest of the team will follow, but only if the two of us lead the charge'."
Du Plessis wrote that his former schoolmate took up the challenge, not only by aggressively "sledging" Smith but by scoring an outstanding century, which helped South Africa win the match and go on to win the series.
Cricket Australia on Saturday threw its "unanimous support" behind Pat Cummins to remain the current Test captain, rejecting any suggestion his integrity had been compromised by the lingering "Sandpapergate" scandal.
Cummins has been under huge pressure since Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the ball-tampering plot but he strenuously denied being aware of what was going on in a press conference last week.

item.title: Bangladesh all out for 91 after SA pace burst
item.description:
Bangladesh were dismissed for 91 in its first innings of the second and final cricket Test against South Africa after putting up a reckless batting show at SuperSport Park in Centurion today.
The South African pace attack caused the damage with Kagso Rabada and Marco Jansen claiming three wickets apiece. Anrich Nortje who unsettled Bangladesh batters with raw pace, returned figures of 2-10 while pacer Wiaan Mulder and left-arm spinner Simon Harmer took one wicket each.
Opener Mahfijul Islam Robin was the top-scorer for the side with 23 while two other batters-Tawhid Hridoy and Mominul Haque-were able to reach double digits, adding 19 and 18 runs respectively.
After rain delayed the toss and washed out the entire first session, Bangladesh found them in vulnerable state in a pitch offering considerable seam movement and bounce.
But Bangladesh batters, after being asked to bat first, failed to show the patience required to hang around.
The rot began with the dismissal of Tanzid Hasan Tamim who edged Jansen to first slip by poking a delivery outside off.
Another opener Mahifjul Isalm Robin played some confident shots against the Bangladesh nemesis Kagsio Rabada to give the side some hopes.
But Nortje came up with raw pace to unsettle the Bangladesh batters. He removed Mahfijul for 23 and skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto for 4, with express delivery to leave Bangladesh 44-3.
After struggling against Nortje, Mominul finally was removed for 18 by Wiaan Mulder while Jansen claimed the wicket to Liton Das for 8 to deepen Bangladesh's crisis.
Inform Tawhid Hridoy hung around some times and also hit a six against left-arm spinner Simon Harmer. But his aggressive approach cost his wicket as he was dismissed by Harmer on the stroke to tea.
Kagiso Rabada returned to his second spell clean up the tail with three wickets before Jansen wrapped up Bangladesh innings by dismissing Khaled Ahmed for duck.

item.title: Towards stronger ties with Australia
item.description:
We are encouraged by the high-level discussions that took place last Sunday between Foreign Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury and Australian High Commissioner Susan Ryle at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The discussion, centring on trade, investment, energy security, skills development, and labour mobility, signal an encouraging momentum in Dhaka-Canberra relations.
As Bangladesh navigates complex macroeconomic pressures and seeks to diversify its international partnerships, deepening engagement with a major economy like Australia is an opportunity we cannot afford to treat as routine diplomatic pleasantry.
Australia’s historical goodwill toward Bangladesh, dating back to its early recognition of our independence in 1972, is well documented. With that said, diplomatic warmth alone does not generate foreign direct investment, resolve energy deficits, or create jobs.
At this moment in time, attracting credible Australian capital and technical expertise would be of immense value to our economic recovery, as would focusing on education, vocational training, and skilled migration.
With nearly a third of our educated youth facing unemployment while domestic remittances remain a critical pillar of macroeconomic stability, structured mobility pathways and Australian-accredited technical partnerships could transform Bangladesh’s workforce into a competitive global asset.
However, bilateral potential with any and all nations repeatedly stalls when confronted with domestic institutional bottlenecks - and is a reality that we must not just confront but overcome.
Australian investors will not commit long-term capital if they continue to encounter red tape, bureaucratic inertia, energy unreliability, or erratic tax policies.
The government therefore must move swiftly from courtesy calls to concrete, time-bound frameworks. Strengthening ties with Australia is an undeniable positive but the onus is on the government to execute the reforms required to make this partnership truly count.

item.title: Rebalancing the tax burden
item.description:
A recent study by the Research and Policy Integration for Development (RAPID) has sparked a necessary debate over fairness in Bangladesh’s fiscal system, finding that the poorest 10% of households pay value-added tax (VAT) equivalent to one-fifth of their reported income compared to just 2.8% for the wealthiest 10%.
As such, while the authors responsibly noted methodological caveats, including the likelihood of income underreporting in household surveys and a more proportionate picture when measured against consumption expenditure, the underlying structural reality remains troubling and one we have known for a long time: Our tax system leans far too heavily on regressive consumption taxes that disproportionately squeeze low-income citizens.
As experts have opined and this newspaper has editorialized numerous times, mobilizing public revenue must go beyond chasing arbitrary collection targets; it must uphold fairness, transparency, and public trust.
Currently, Bangladesh’s tax-to-GDP ratio languishes around 7% -- one of the lowest in the region -- largely because direct taxation remains chronically under-enforced. Despite earning over 40% of total household income and accounting for more than 93% of potential personal income tax, the wealthiest decile largely escapes the net.
Crucially, experts agree that Bangladesh does not need to invent punitive new levies to fix its fiscal deficit. Simply enforcing compliance with existing income tax and domestic VAT laws could be transformative.
While Finance Secretary Md Khairuzzaman Mozumder assuring that the government will examine progressive income tax restructuring, realistic market-based land valuations, and surcharge adjustments to address these issues is a welcome starting point, intent must translate into decisive execution.
An equitable society cannot be built by disproportionately taxing the daily necessities of its poorest citizens while high earners slip through regulatory cracks. True fiscal reform demands shifting the burden so that every citizen contributes in fair proportion to their means.

item.title: Calmer winter seas bring growing fears of human trafficking
item.description:
During a visit to Teknaf last month, I spoke with residents and religious leaders about what worried them as winter approached.
One religious leader feared that calmer seas would make it easier for smugglers and traffickers to launch boats from the Teknaf coast. As we talked, the conversation turned to decisions families face on land.
When work is scarce, a broker’s promise of a job abroad can be hard to turn down. When someone disappears, their family may have no idea where to look or whom to call.
Both concerns surfaced on November 20, 2026, when law enforcement officers rescued 28 people from a trawler that had reached Laboni Point in Cox’s Bazar.
Some survivors said they had been lured with promises of passage to Malaysia. Others said they had been abducted at gunpoint in Teknaf.
Survivors also reported beatings and demands for ransom. Weeks earlier, a ninth-grade student had been abducted, held for weeks and sold from one broker to another before being put aboard a trawler.
His account points to a period when a family’s report could help investigators search for someone on land.
The winter sailing season is a concern for people on shore. The International Organization for Migration says sea crossings typically pick up again in November. Its 2026 assessment warned that worsening conditions in the Cox’s Bazar camps and continued conflict in Myanmar’s Rakhine State could push more Rohingya refugees to attempt the journey.
UNHCR recorded more than 6,500 Rohingya refugees attempting dangerous crossings in 2025, with nearly 900 reported dead or missing in the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea. Calmer conditions make it easier to set out. The accounts from Laboni Point show the dangers people can face once aboard, whatever brought them there.
For those of us who work with communities, an awareness session should prepare people for a decision they might actually face. At a school assembly, a youth group meeting, or a courtyard discussion with parents, we can walk through a familiar example: A broker offers a job abroad and asks for money that day. Who is the employer? Is there a written contract? Is the recruiter licensed?
Teachers and religious leaders can show families how to check the license in the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training’s register. A short Bangla handout can give families a place to seek advice before paying or handing over documents.
A suspected abduction or confinement calls for urgent action. Humanitarian organi z ations and local police should agree on named police contact for urgent reports and tell families how to follow up.
Community leaders can help families pass on details such as the last known location, the broker’s number or a ransom message directly to police.
In the Rohingya camps, protection teams can offer a confidential way to report threats and help people reach the appropriate authorities. Police should look for links across reports of disappearances, confinement, and ransom demands. A detail from one family may help investigators act on another family’s report.
That cooperation should continue after a rescue. Someone who paid a smuggler to cross a border may have faced threats or exploitation during the journey. Someone else may have been forced aboard from the start.
Police and humanitarian workers should speak with survivors privately and arrange support according to their needs, including medical care, safe contact with family, and specialist referrals for children.
This winter, teachers, religious leaders and humanitarian workers can help families check job offers and know how to report a suspected abduction. When a family raises the alarm, they should have someone they trust to turn to and a clear way to get help while there is still time to search on land.
Md Shihabul Hossain works as Deputy Manager with BRAC Migration Program. The views expressed are personal.

item.title: The middle class is vanishing. Who will rescue them?
item.description:
For several decades, most Bangladeshis have had the same aspirations. To graduate from university, get a reasonably good job, purchase a home, put your children through higher education in another country, look after your aging parents, and eventually retire with dignity.
We are not dreaming of extravagant wealth here. We are simply dreaming of a level of financial security and stability that we are rapidly losing.
Pay day is followed by one’s obligations to pay the monthly rent, buy groceries, pay school fees, transportation and utility bills, etc. One unexpected major expense (for example, a major medical procedure) can quickly wipe out one’s savings.
Although some families are experiencing an increase in overall income, even for them, after these expenditures are made, they are left with very little, if any, spending money for the month.
Recent World Bank reports indicate that during FY 2026, an additional 2.1 million people are projected to be in poverty. Further, during this same period, the national poverty rate in Bangladesh increased from 18.7% to an estimated 21.4%.
We are now faced with the much greater challenge of keeping previously elevated living standards attained by some of the population from slipping back into poverty.
Meanwhile, for the poorest of the population, increasing costs of production can rapidly change their lives for the worse whereas for the wealthy, such increases may be little more than minor inconveniences.
The average monthly income of urban households (based on the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ Living Standard Survey of 2025) is Tk 33,513, and the average monthly expenditure of human households in Bangladesh stands at Tk 35,311 ( an average monthly deficit of Tk 1,798).
During this period, 47% of the households in our survey were reported to have taken out loans to meet their living expenses. These numbers demonstrate the financial challenges faced by families in Bangladesh.
Families may be stretched financially so much that they are unable to purchase school supplies, have no other way of supporting children through education to attain employment, and are thus unable to secure a better future for them.
A part of this salary crisis that has been overlooked is the fact that middle class spending is as much about aspiration as it is about consumption. Middle class parents send their children to better schools in order to create more opportunities for them in the future. They also spend money on coaching to increase their child’s chances of getting through better universities.
Another growing concern for families in Bangladesh is the cost of housing. In Dhaka, for example, to meet monthly expenses, many families have to move to smaller apartments or endure extremely long commutes from workplaces.
While the rent may be low, the opportunity cost ( lost time, stress, and/or distance from schools, hospitals, etc) associated with that location may be quite high.
We believe that with good financial security, middle class households should be able to set aside savings during periods of sickness or unemployment to enable them to educate their children. However, given the ongoing increases in prices, this is becoming increasingly difficult to achieve.
In October 2026, the average nominal wage growth rate (7.63%) was also lower than the general inflation rate (8.27%) indicating that, in real terms, wages decreased during this period. If we assume a household is able to save Tk 10,000 each month, they will still be at a financial loss to meet their monthly expenses if, for example, costs of education and/or health services increase.
Of likely greater concern to most households is the impact of inflation on the family’s ability to save/take out loans to finance larger purchases to ensure they achieve their goal of economic mobility.
Based on current information available to us, any realistic scenario for addressing the current middle class crisis in Bangladesh would need to incorporate measures to improve the overall wage level for the population as a whole, in addition to increasing the level of investment and productivity in the economy.
We understand that the missing middle class in Bangladesh is largely due to the overall economic slowdown. Bangladesh should also be proactive to encourage and empower females to participate in the economy.
It is evident that no single policy will likely result in an immediate transformation. While inflation control is arguably the most important thing we can do now, simply controlling inflation will not solve the situation of the middle class. Further improvements to the economy( better job opportunities, better public health and education facilities, improved public transport, etc) are also needed.
Looking ahead
For decades, the middle class of Bangladesh has lived with a certain promise -- to work hard today to give his children an easier future.
A father delays purchasing his own house to pay for his children’s education. A mother deprives herself of the ordinary pleasures of life in order to save up for her children. A young man works overtime every week in the vain hope that one day, his family will not have to count every single taka to determine whether they will be able to make it through this month.
What happens to this family when the sudden need for additional expenses exhausts their accumulated savings? When they realize that no amount of additional work will improve their situation? When they begin to believe that their children will not have a better life than they did?
These are the true tragedies of a diminishing middle class. It’s not just losing your means of economic survival. It means slowly losing hope for the future.
We must do all we can to preserve hope, especially among the millions of families that struggle to just get by. All they have ever wanted is the right to live and to be able to dream of a better future for their families.
If in the future, we look back on the development of Bangladesh and are unable to find sufficient examples of fathers and mothers being able to rest easy at night, knowing their family is safe and secure, then we should question how prosperous our country really is.
Yemad Fayed is a PR professional.

item.title: Death toll from Indonesia factory fire rises to 24
item.description:
A fire that tore through a confectionery factory west of Indonesia’s capital Jakarta has killed at least 24 people, police said Monday, revising an earlier toll after rescuers retrieved bodies from the rubble.
The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in the Serang district around 50 kilometers from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon trapping workers inside.
“There are 24 bodies” that the rescuers retrieved since the Saturday blaze, local police chief Moehamad Probandono Bobby Danuardi told reporters.
Rescuers had previously said 34 people were unaccounted for after the incident, which also injured five people.
The agency had yet to provide an updated death toll since Sunday morning when it initially confirmed three people were killed in the blaze.
Said Iqbal, the presidential advisor for workers’ welfare, said in a statement Monday that a short circuit in the building’s AC system could have been behind the blaze, but stressed that further investigation must be carried out to determine the cause of the incident.
Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.
A blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion in December last year tore through a seven-story building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.
And at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east in 2023 after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

item.title: Dhaka Board extends deadline for 2027 SSC form submission
item.description:
The Dhaka Education Board has extended the deadline for filling out forms for the 2027 Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examinations.
According to a notice issued by the board on Monday, the deadline was extended considering the academic interests of the examinees. Under the revised schedule, candidates will be able to fill out their forms online without a late fee until November 28, while the deadline for submitting fees online without a late fee is November 29.
Besides, online form submission with a late fee will be allowed from November 30 to December 5. The last date for submitting fees online with a late fee of Tk100 per candidate has been set for December 6.
The principals and head teachers of all SSC-level educational institutions under the board have been instructed to complete the form submission process for their students within the stipulated deadlines.

item.title: Dark mode or light mode: Which one is actually better for your eyes?
item.description:
Whether on a mobile phone, laptop, or desktop computer, many people spend a significant part of their day looking at screens. Prolonged screen time can leave the eyes feeling tired, dry, and uncomfortable.
To ease this discomfort, many users switch their devices to dark mode, believing that white text on a black background puts less strain on the eyes. But does dark mode really make a difference? Is it always the better choice?
According to experts, the answer depends on several factors, including lighting conditions, surroundings, and individual vision. Simply keeping dark mode on all the time does not necessarily mean better eye health.
The pupil, the black opening at the center of the eye, changes size depending on the amount of light entering the eye. In dim surroundings, the pupil expands to let in more light. However, a larger pupil can slightly reduce the eye's ability to focus sharply on objects.
In brighter conditions, the pupil becomes smaller, allowing the eyes to see text and images more clearly.
This is why reading small white letters against a black background in a dark room can sometimes put extra strain on the eyes. Although the screen may feel more comfortable, smaller text can become harder to read.
On the other hand, using a mobile phone or laptop with all the room lights switched off can make a bright screen feel particularly harsh. Every time you look away from the screen and then return to it, your pupils have to adjust to the changing light. This repeated adjustment may cause discomfort.
Since dark mode produces less overall screen light, it may help reduce this discomfort in low-light environments.
A 2021 study published in the journal IEEE Access found that people tended to blink more frequently while using dark mode. Based on their findings, the researchers suggested using dark mode at night. However, many participants reported experiencing less eye fatigue in light mode and preferred it over dark mode.
Bright light in the evening, particularly blue light, can interfere with the production of melatonin, the hormone that helps regulate sleep.
However, the amount of blue light emitted by a screen depends on factors such as screen brightness and the type of content being viewed.
Reducing the brightness of your phone or laptop in the evening can help make screen use more comfortable. You can also use features such as Night Shift or a blue-light filter.
Still, the best habit is to avoid using screens altogether before bedtime.
In daylight or brightly lit office environments, reading black text against a white background is generally easier. This is known as the positive polarity advantage .
A 2013 study published in the journal Ergonomics found that reading in light mode offered advantages for both younger and older adults.
Another study, published in Human Factors in 2014, suggested that the smaller the text, the greater the reading advantage of light mode.
In light mode, the bright background helps keep the pupils relatively constricted, making letters appear sharper and easier to distinguish. This can be particularly helpful when reading small text.
Not every screen setting works equally well for everyone. Individual eye conditions can influence which mode feels more comfortable.
For example, people with astigmatism may find that white letters in dark mode appear to have a glowing halo around them. This can make text look blurry or cause letters to appear as though they are merging.
On the other hand, people with certain conditions, such as cataracts, may find dark mode more comfortable.
A 2025 study published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health , involving 30 female tablet users, found no significant difference in eye fatigue between dark and light modes. However, participants reported fewer symptoms of dry eyes when using dark mode.
Still, these findings do not establish dark mode as the healthier option for everyone. While it may offer relief in certain situations, the benefits can vary from person to person.
Dark mode can make screens more comfortable, particularly in dimly lit surroundings. However, it cannot eliminate the eye strain associated with prolonged digital device use.
For some people, it may even make reading more difficult. Switching to dark mode does not automatically protect against dry eyes or retinal damage.
Rather than relying solely on display settings, developing healthier screen habits is essential for maintaining eye comfort.
Here are some simple habits worth following:
The 20-20-20 rule is a simple technique that can help reduce digital eye strain. It encourages people to shift their focus away from nearby screens at regular intervals.
The rule is straightforward: After every 20 minutes of screen time, look at something approximately 20 feet (around six meters) away for at least 20 seconds.
You can set a reminder on your phone or computer to follow this routine. Look out of a window or towards an object at the other end of the room. Remember to blink a few times while doing so.
This simple habit may help reduce eye dryness and discomfort associated with prolonged screen use.
There is no one-size-fits-all answer. Dark mode may be a more comfortable option in the evening or in dimly lit environments, while light mode generally makes reading easier during the day or in brightly lit spaces.
Adjusting screen brightness to match your surroundings and increasing text size can also make a noticeable difference.
Ultimately, protecting your eyes is not just about choosing between a black or white background. Taking regular breaks, blinking frequently, and developing healthier screen habits are far more important for long-term eye comfort.

item.title: Five health benefits of eating raw turmeric every morning
item.description:
Raw turmeric has long been popular as a natural ingredient and has been widely used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine. According to experts, chewing a small piece of raw turmeric every morning on an empty stomach may offer several health benefits. However, it is best to consume it in moderation rather than in excessive amounts.
Raw turmeric contains curcumin, a compound that may help support the body's immune system. Consuming small amounts regularly may help reduce the risk of seasonal illnesses, such as colds and coughs, and certain infections.
Raw turmeric may play a role in reducing inflammation in the body. It can be particularly beneficial for people experiencing joint pain or mild inflammatory conditions, thanks to its anti-inflammatory properties.
Consuming raw turmeric in the morning may help support healthy digestion. It is also believed to help relieve digestive discomfort, including gas and bloating.
The antioxidant properties of raw turmeric may help maintain healthy skin. Regular consumption in moderate amounts may contribute to a natural glow by helping protect the body against oxidative stress.
According to experts, raw turmeric may help support normal liver function and assist the body's natural processes for eliminating harmful substances.
However, people with gallstones, those taking blood-thinning medications, or individuals with other chronic health conditions should consult a doctor before making raw turmeric a regular part of their diet. Consuming too much raw turmeric may also cause stomach discomfort or acidity.

item.description:

Convener of the Bangladesh-Pakistan Parliamentary Friendship Group of Pakistan's National Assembly Dr Shazia Sobia Aslam Soomro and Bangladesh High Commissioner to Pakistan Md Iqbal Hussain Khan were also present at the airport to welcome the him, said a press release.

item.title: GSTU students erase graffiti seeking justice for July uprising, Hadi
item.description:
Graffiti demanding justice for the July uprising and the killings of Sharif Osman Hadi, along with other slogans, were erased at Gopalganj Science and Technology University (GSTU) on Monday by students accused of having links to the activities-banned Bangladesh Chhatra League.
The slogans were removed around 1pm from the university's main gate, areas around the open stage and several locations on the administrative building.
Those seen removing the graffiti included Mahfuzur Rahman Shuvo, a 2021-22 academic-year student of the Department of Law; Mehedi and Sikdar Joy, both from the 2022-23 session of the same department; Irfan Sajid of the 2023-24 session; and Abid of the 2021-22 session of the Department of International Relations. Several other students were also present.
Explaining their actions, they said Hadi had made derogatory remarks about Gopalganj and that they did not want anything associated with him to remain in the district or on the university campus.
Asked about their political affiliations, they denied having any and described themselves as ordinary university students, adding that all those who took part in the activity were from Gopalganj.
Several attempts were made to contact university Proctor Dr SM Ahsan by phone for comment, but he did not answer. His comments could not be obtained.
